title: Paragraphs out of a PDF
problem: Our office copies paragraphs out of UN PDFs by hand. Can a tool split a General Comment into its numbered paragraphs and footnotes, and show me where it got things wrong?
facilitator_brief: The file is the raw text of CESCR General comment No. 27 as a PDF converter produced it, page by page, with a reference (paragraph and footnote counts, first words of each paragraph). The tool must check itself against the reference and make every repair it makes visible.
notes:
The problem, as I read it: an office copies paragraphs out of UN PDFs by hand and wants a tool that splits a document into its paragraphs and footnotes and, just as important, shows where it went wrong. The facilitator sets the standard: check the result against the reference, and make every repair visible. The data is one document, CESCR General comment No. 27, as 20 pages of raw converter output, plus a reference block with the paragraph count, the footnote count and the first six words of each paragraph.

 The overview: 20 records, one per page, two fields, `page` and `text`; the top-level `count` is the string "20". The reference says 90 paragraphs, 141 footnotes, adopted 26 September 2025.  Page 1 shows the converter's habits at once. A paragraph number stands alone on its line ("1.", a line break, then "A clean, healthy…"); a section heading is split into "I.", a blank line and "Introduction"; footnote references are glued to the word before them ("waste.2") or set off by a space ("”. 3"); the footnote block at the foot of the page opens with a bare "1" on its own line, then the text, while the next footnotes read "2 Summary for policymakers…".  Page 2 opens with the header "E/C.12/GC/27" and the rest of paragraph 2, so paragraphs cross pages and the pages must be joined before the text is split. Its footnotes held a surprise: footnote 6 reads "A/42/427, p. 24." with no number, and a bare "6" turns up at the very end of the page, next to the page number.

 Counting: 88 lines are a number and a full stop alone.  Allowing any whitespace after the stop gives 90, the document's count,  and the two extra are paragraphs 23 and 87, whose number and text share a line ("23. The full realization…"). A rule for one form alone misses two or finds two.  Bare numbers on a line: 51, of three kinds: the page number in the footer (2 to 20), the first footnote on each page, and displaced footnote numbers like that "6". The footer comes in two orders, "page, GE code" and "GE code, page".  The last page ends with paragraph 90, footnotes 139 to 141 and the footer, nothing after.  Lines that start with a number and a space: 110; one is "6 November 2025" on the cover, the rest are footnotes.  No lettered sub-paragraphs "(a)": the paragraphs are plain prose, 43 to 254 words each.

I then ran these rules in a short script of my own. Dropping each page's header line, footer lines and footnote block, joining the rest and splitting at the paragraph numbers gives exactly 90 paragraphs, numbered 1 to 90 without a gap, and all 90 first six words match the reference once curly quotes and spacing are normalised. Footnotes: 129 start with their number; the 12 missing numbers (6, 14, 45, 51, 67, 76, 87, 96, 101, 115, 118, 131) are exactly the bare numbers displaced to the page foot, one per page, so 129 + 12 = 141. Inside the paragraphs, all 141 footnote marks can be recovered only with a sequential rule: walk through the text and accept a number when it is the next one expected. A rule based on punctuation alone finds 134 and misses marks after a comma ("equity, 17 common"); the sequential rule rejects four real numbers ("Articles 1 (2) and 25", "article 11", "arts. 13 and 14"), all correctly. Two more traps: 23 unlabelled headings such as "Right to work (art. 6)" and "Children" stand on the line just before a paragraph number and are glued to the end of the previous paragraph unless a rule catches them; and the labelled headings wrap ("III." has a two-line title). Nineteen paragraphs span a page break.

Then the shelf.  A search on PDF cleaning found nothing on the subject; the shelf is about presenting results, not converters.  A search on quality assurance led to the Analysis Function's page on testing code.  Accessible tables: four pages, the Analysis Function's first.  Citing UN documents: the Dag Hammarskjöld Library's answer.  The testing page gave the check panel its shape: tests that tell a story, "given this data, having run this code, we expect this output", and a new test for every bug found, which here means a named check for every repair the script makes.  The clear-language page: short sentences, explain a specialist term the first time, "must" for a requirement.  The tables page: right-aligned numbers, a title that states the message, the source under the table, no footnotes in data cells.  A search on working with AI assistants brought back the testing page and the Claude Code best practices, whose fifth point is the same lesson: give the machine a check that returns pass or fail.  The Library's page lists what a citation carries, the symbol first and the paragraph as the pinpoint; the citation form became a question.

Trade-offs. The script repairs only the damage I found, names each repair on screen and guesses nothing. The reference is the yardstick, not the truth: the app shows its own count next to the document's and never adjusts a result to match. No model calls; nothing leaves the browser. The five questions are the office's choices, not mine: footnote marks, headings, footnote text, citation form, line breaks.

questions.question: What should happen to the footnote numbers that sit inside the paragraph text, such as "waste.2"?

options.label: Bracket them
options.description: Each mark becomes [2] in the shown text and in the CSV, so a reader sees where the footnotes were and can remove them with one find-and-replace.

fragments.text: Footnote marks inside the text are shown in square brackets, "waste.[2]", in the table, the expanded paragraph and the CSV; a note under the table says so and gives the pattern `\[\d+\]` for removing them with find-and-replace.

- **Footnote marks in the text.** Only a sequential rule tells a mark from a real number such as "article 11". Walk through each paragraph's text in document order with a counter that starts at 1. Every run of one to three digits not touching another digit, a slash, a dash or an opening parenthesis is a candidate; a candidate equal to the counter is a mark and the counter goes up by one; any other number is left alone. Each mark becomes `[n]`, the character before it kept ("waste.[2]", "equity,[17] common"). `text_raw` keeps the unmodified text.

- **Footnote marks.** Marks found in the paragraphs, expected to run from 1 to `reference.footnotes` without a gap; the check lists any missing numbers and the numbers it rejected as not being marks (with context), so the reader can see that "article 11" was not bracketed.

options.label: Strip them
options.description: The paragraph text is cleaned of the marks for quoting; the marks found are kept in a separate column so nothing is removed silently.

fragments.text: Footnote marks are removed from the text shown in the table, the expanded paragraph and the CSV; a column "Footnotes cited" lists the numbers removed from each paragraph ("1, 2"), and a note under the table says that the shown text is cleaned and that `text_raw` in the CSV keeps the marks.

- **Footnote marks in the text.** Only a sequential rule tells a mark from a real number such as "article 11". Walk through each paragraph's text in document order with a counter that starts at 1. Every run of one to three digits that is not touching another digit, a slash, a dash or an opening parenthesis is a candidate; a candidate equal to the counter is a footnote mark and the counter goes up by one. Any other number is left alone. Each mark is deleted together with the single space before it when there is one ("waste.2" becomes "waste."). The numbers removed go to `footnotes_cited`; `text_raw` keeps the unmodified text.

- **Footnote marks.** Marks removed from the paragraphs, expected to run from 1 to `reference.footnotes` without a gap; the check lists any missing numbers and the numbers it rejected as not being marks (with context), so the reader can confirm that "article 11" was not removed.

options.label: Leave them
options.description: The text stays exactly as the converter produced it, marks glued to words and all; the app only counts the marks it can see.

fragments.text: The paragraph text is shown exactly as the converter produced it, footnote marks included ("waste.2"); a note under the table says that the digits glued to words are footnote references, not part of the text.

- **Footnote marks in the text** are counted but not changed. Walk through each paragraph's text in document order with a counter that starts at 1. Every run of one to three digits that is not touching another digit, a slash, a dash or an opening parenthesis is a candidate; a candidate equal to the counter is a footnote mark and the counter goes up by one. Any other number is left alone. The count per paragraph goes to `footnotes_cited`; the text is stored once, unmodified.

- **Footnote marks.** Marks counted in the paragraphs, expected to run from 1 to `reference.footnotes` without a gap; the check lists any missing numbers, so the reader knows how many references hide in the text they will paste.

questions.question: What should the app do with the document's section headings, such as "Right to work (art. 6)"?

options.label: Section column
options.description: Each paragraph gets the heading it sits under, in a table column and in the CSV; headings never appear inside paragraph text.

fragments.text: A **Section** column, between No. and Page, shows the nearest heading above each paragraph ("Right to work (art. 6)"); the expanded paragraph shows the full path ("IV. … › Right to work (art. 6)"). A collapsible "Headings found: n" box above the table lists them, so the reader can see that none was swallowed into a paragraph.
Each paragraph's `section` is the most recent heading line before it and `part` the most recent roman-numbered heading; a heading line is never part of a paragraph's text.

options.label: Heading rows
options.description: Headings appear as their own grey rows in the table, in document order, so the table reads like the document's table of contents; the CSV gets a "kind" column.

fragments.text: Headings appear in the table as rows of their own, in document order, grey, bold and unnumbered, and marked "heading" in a **Kind** column for screen readers, so the table reads like the document's table of contents and a reader sees where each heading was found. The CSV has the same rows with `kind` set to "heading" or "paragraph".

Heading lines become records of their own with `kind` "heading", their `label` ("IV.", "A." or empty) and their text, placed in document order between the paragraphs; a heading line is never part of a paragraph's text.

questions.question: Should the app also extract the text of the footnotes, not only keep them out of the paragraphs?

options.label: Extract them
options.description: A second table lists every footnote with its number and text, and the expanded paragraph shows the footnotes it cites.

fragments.text: A table, "Footnotes found: n of `reference.footnotes`", with columns No. | Page | Text | Repair, where Repair reads "number restored from the page foot" for a footnote whose number the converter displaced. The expanded paragraph also lists the footnotes it cites. A download button, "footnotes.csv", on this tab.

- **Footnote text.** Inside each page's footnote block, a line that starts with a number and a space, or a bare number on its own line, opens a footnote; the lines up to the next opener are its text, joined with a space. Any line that starts with a number and a space opens a footnote, even when the number is not the one expected: never add a numbered line to the footnote before it. On a page with a displaced number D, the first footnote (its bare number, a blank line, then its text) ends at its first line that ends with a full stop; the lines after it, up to the next numbered line, are footnote D, marked `repaired`. The cover's asterisked note is kept as footnote "*" and not counted.

- **Footnotes.** Footnotes found (numbered openers plus restored numbers) against `reference.footnotes`; the numbers run from 1 to that count without a gap or a duplicate; the restored numbers are listed with their page as repairs.

options.label: Count only
options.description: Footnotes are removed from the paragraphs and counted against the reference; their text is not shown.

fragments.text: One line: "Footnotes removed from the pages: n of `reference.footnotes`; their text is not extracted in this version", with a collapsible list of the pages and the number of footnote lines cut from each.

- **Footnote text** is not extracted. Inside each page's footnote block, lines that start with a number and a space, or are a bare number, count as footnote openers; a number displaced to the page foot counts as one more footnote and is logged as a repair. The block's text is discarded.
- **Footnotes.** Footnote openers found in the removed blocks plus restored numbers, against `reference.footnotes`; the restored numbers are listed with their page as repairs.

questions.question: How should each paragraph be cited in the table and the CSV?

options.label: Symbol and paragraph
options.description: The short form used in UN practice: the document symbol, then "para." and the number, as in "E/C.12/GC/27, para. 12".

fragments.text: and a **Copy citation** button that copies "`symbol`, para. n" (for example "E/C.12/GC/27, para. 12") and shows "Copied" for two seconds; the same string is the CSV's `citation` column.
- **Citation** = `symbol` + ", para. " + the paragraph number, with `symbol` read from `WORKSHOP_DATA.pdf_text`, never typed in.

options.label: Full reference
options.description: Everything the UN Library recommends: title, symbol, adoption date, paragraph, the UN link and the date you accessed it.

fragments.text: and a **Copy citation** button that copies the full reference, "Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, `title`, `symbol` (adopted `reference.adopted`), para. n, `doc_url` (accessed today's date)", and shows "Copied" for two seconds; the same string is the CSV's `citation` column, and the header says which style is applied.

- **Citation** is assembled from fields, never typed in: `title`, `symbol` and `doc_url` from `WORKSHOP_DATA.pdf_text`, `reference.adopted`, the paragraph number, and the access date from `new Date()` as day, month name, year. The CSV also carries each part in its own column (`adopted`, `accessed`).

questions.question: Should a paragraph be one block of text, or keep the PDF's line breaks?

options.label: One block
options.description: The converter's line breaks are replaced by single spaces, so a paragraph pastes into a document as one paragraph.

fragments.text: The expanded paragraph is one block of running text; a "Show the PDF's lines" toggle under it reveals the same text with the converter's line breaks and the page number where each page began, so the join can be checked.

- **Paragraph text** = the paragraph's lines joined with a single space, double spaces collapsed, trimmed. No line in the file ends with a hyphen, so no hyphen joining is done; the app counts such lines anyway and reports the number. `text_lines` keeps the original lines for the toggle and the CSV column `text_lines` (lines separated by " | ").

options.label: Keep breaks
options.description: The lines stay as the PDF had them, so a reader can compare against the original line by line; the CSV cell holds the breaks too.

fragments.text: The expanded paragraph keeps the converter's line breaks (a wrapping `<pre>`-like block) with a thin rule and the page number where a new page began, so a reader can compare line by line with the PDF; a "Copy as one paragraph" button gives the joined form for pasting.

- **Paragraph text** keeps the converter's lines, separated by a newline; the CSV cell holds the newlines inside its quotes (RFC 4180 allows it; Excel and LibreOffice read it). The joined form, lines joined with a single space and double spaces collapsed, is computed for the first-words check and the copy button. No line in the file ends with a hyphen; the app counts such lines anyway and reports the number in the check panel.

plan_base:
# Paragraphs out of a PDF: the numbered paragraphs of a General Comment, checked against the reference

## Context

The user works in an office that quotes UN documents: a national human rights institution, an NGO or a mission in Geneva. To cite a General Comment they open the PDF, copy the paragraph by hand, remove the footnote numbers and page headers that come with it, and type the citation. A PDF converter copies in a second but damages the text in four ways: it reorders (a footnote number lands at the foot of the page), breaks (a paragraph across two pages), loses (the number of footnote 6) and adds noise (headers, footers, date stamps). This app turns the converter's raw text of one document, `WORKSHOP_DATA.pdf_text`, into numbered paragraphs, compares the result with the document's own reference, and shows every repair it made. The pages are `records` (`page`, `text`); the yardstick is `reference` (`paragraphs`, `footnotes`, `adopted`, `first_words`); `title`, `symbol` and `doc_url` describe the document. Nothing is typed in by hand.

## What I found in the data

The numbers come from the file I examined; the app computes its own from the file it is given.

- 20 pages, `text` filled on every page, 2,800 to 4,300 characters each; `count` is the string "20". `reference.paragraphs` is 90, `reference.footnotes` 141; `reference.first_words` is keyed by the paragraph number as a string.
- **Header.** The first line of every page is the document symbol.
- **Footer.** The last lines of a page are, in varying order, the page number alone on a line (pages 2 to 20) and the job code "GE.25-15926"; page 1 has "GE.25-15926 (E)" and a date stamp "051125 061125" instead. On 12 pages a third bare number sits in the footer: a footnote number the converter displaced (6, 14, 45, 51, 67, 76, 87, 96, 101, 115, 118, 131); that footnote's text on the page has no number.
- **Paragraph numbers.** 88 of 90 stand alone on their line ("1." then the text on the next line); 2 (paragraphs 23 and 87) share the line with their text. A rule for one form alone misses the other.
- **Headings.** Roman-numbered sections ("I.", a blank line, "Introduction") and lettered subsections ("A.") whose title can wrap over two lines; and 23 unlabelled headings ("Right to work (art. 6)", "Children") on the line just before a paragraph number, so a naive split glues them to the previous paragraph.
- **Footnotes.** Each page's footnotes sit at the foot, before the footer. The first on a page is a bare number on its own line, a blank line, then the text; the others are "7 E/2003/22…". 129 start with their number; 12 lost it (the displaced numbers above). On each of those 12 pages the footnote without a number is the **second** on the page: it follows the first footnote's text directly, with no number and no blank line (page 2: "5", a blank line, "A/79/270, paras. 84 and 85.", then "A/42/427, p. 24." is footnote 6). In all 12 cases the first footnote is one line ending with a full stop. A parser that only follows the numbers glues the two together, then waits for a number that never comes and loses every footnote after it: on 3 Nov a build found 5 of 141 and left the footnote blocks of 16 pages inside paragraphs. The cover's asterisked note, "* Adopted by the Committee…", is not one of the 141.
- **Footnote marks in the text.** 141 marks, glued to the word before ("waste.2"), after a space ("”. 3") or after a comma ("equity, 17 common"); real numbers such as "article 11" look the same, so only a sequential rule tells them apart.
- 19 paragraphs span a page break; paragraphs are 43 to 254 words of plain prose, no lettered sub-paragraphs, no line ending in a hyphen; curly quotes and en dashes occur, so comparisons normalise them.

## The app, tab by tab

**Header, always visible.** A monospace label "UN DOCUMENT · PDF TEXT", the serif title `title`, one line: `symbol` linked to `doc_url` (new tab), "adopted `reference.adopted`", "n pages of raw converter text", `source`. One sentence under it says what the page does: splits, removes headers, footers and footnotes, checks itself, lists every repair. The footer line (last item below) is also always visible. The app reads one document, so there is no filter rail. Under the header, numbered tabs (`role="tablist"`, arrow keys): `01 RESULT · 02 PARAGRAPHS · 03 FOOTNOTES · 04 CHECKS · 05 METHOD AND EXPORT`.

**01 RESULT. Did the app find everything the document has?** Four tiles with big serif numbers, each with a one-line "How this is computed" note: **Paragraphs found: n** next to **The document has: `reference.paragraphs`** (green when equal, red with the difference); **Footnotes found: n of `reference.footnotes`**; **First words match: n of `reference.paragraphs`**; **Repairs made: n**, a link to the repair log on tab 04. Under the tiles one line, "n of m checks pass", linking to tab 04. Seven things to click: five tabs and two links.

**02 PARAGRAPHS. What does each paragraph say, and how do I cite it?** One row per paragraph: No. | Page | First line | Check: the number right-aligned, the page(s) it starts and ends on ("3–4" across a page break), the first 120 characters cut at a word with "…", and a Check cell reading "OK" or "first words differ" (red; the reference's words appear in the expanded row). {{q2}} {{q1}} Rows are buttons with `aria-expanded`; clicking or pressing Enter expands the row in place, under it.

Under the row, the full text, verbatim as computed, never shortened. {{q5}} Under the text: the reference's first six words next to the extracted first six words, marked equal or different; the page(s); the repairs that touched this paragraph; {{q4}}

**03 FOOTNOTES. What do the footnotes say?** {{q3}}

**04 CHECKS. Can I trust this?** The check panel (see "How the app checks itself"), open, every check on one line. Under it a closed heading "Repair log (n)", a button with `aria-expanded`, which the Repairs tile on tab 01 also opens: a table of every change the script made, in document order, Page | Paragraph or footnote | What was done | Before | After, with a count per kind above it. The kinds are the ones named in the next section: header line removed, footer line removed, number and text split, paragraph joined across a page break, heading separated, heading title joined, footnote number restored, footnote block removed. Six things to click: five tabs and the repair log heading (plus the "rows concerned" link of a failed check).

**05 METHOD AND EXPORT. How was it done, and can I take it away?** The raw page viewer: a select "Show raw page n" and a monospaced panel with the page's `text` as stored, line numbers on the left, each line coloured by what the script decided it was (cover, header, heading, paragraph, footnote, footer), with a legend. Then **Download**: "Download paragraphs as CSV", one row per paragraph with `number`, `section`, `part`, `page_start`, `page_end`, `first_words_reference`, `first_words_found`, `first_words_match`, `text`, `text_raw`, `footnotes_cited`, `repairs`, `citation`, `symbol`, `doc_url`; UTF-8 with a byte-order mark, every field double-quoted with inner quotes doubled, CRLF line ends, a Blob URL, file name from the symbol with slashes replaced by hyphens. Seven things to click: five tabs, the select and the download.

**Footer, always visible.** Source line, `built` date, and "Counting, splitting and matching are done by this page's code; no model was called and nothing left the browser."

## How every number is computed

The pipeline runs once on load, in this order, over `records` sorted by `page`; each step logs what it removed or changed.

- **Header.** If a page's first non-empty line equals `symbol`, drop it and log "header line removed"; otherwise log a warning for that page.
- **Footer.** From the end of each page, drop lines while the line is empty, starts with "GE." (the job code), consists only of 6-digit groups (the date stamp), or is a bare number of one to three digits. A bare number equal to `page` is the page number; any other is a **displaced footnote number**, kept aside for that page.
- **Footnote block.** Keep a counter `nextFootnote`, starting at 1. On each page, after header and footer are gone, the block starts at the first line that is a bare number equal to `nextFootnote`, or starts with that number and a space, or starts with "* " on the first page; from there to the end of the page is footnotes, everything before is body. Advance `nextFootnote` past the highest number seen in the block and past any displaced number for that page. If no line on a page opens `nextFootnote`, take the first bare number greater than it that stands before the footer and log the jump; one missed number must never stop the count on the pages that follow. A page with no opener at all (none here) is all body, and the check panel says so.
{{q3.compute}}
- **Body lines of all pages are concatenated** in page order, each line tagged with its page; this joins the paragraphs that cross a page break (logged as "paragraph joined across a page break" when a paragraph's lines carry two page numbers).
- **Paragraph starts.** A line matching `/^(\d{1,3})\.$/` (number alone) or `/^(\d{1,3})\. (.+)$/` (number and text on one line; the text after the space is the first line, logged as "number and text split"). Lines before the first paragraph start are the cover.
- **Headings.** A line matching `/^([IVX]+|[A-Z])\.$/` opens a labelled heading: skip blank lines, then every line up to the next label line or paragraph start is heading text; a line starting with a lowercase letter or "(" continues the previous heading line (logged as "heading title joined from two lines"), any other line is a further heading. An **unlabelled heading** is a non-empty line immediately followed by a paragraph-start line, at most 90 characters, starting with a capital letter and not ending with a full stop, semicolon, colon, comma or digit (logged as "heading separated from paragraph text"). {{q2.compute}}
- **Paragraph lines.** Every other non-empty body line belongs to the current paragraph; blank lines are dropped. `page_start` and `page_end` are the pages of its first and last line.
{{q5.compute}}
{{q1.compute}}
- **First words.** `first_words_found` = the first six whitespace-separated words of the joined text, footnote marks removed first; `first_words_reference` = `reference.first_words[String(number)]`. They match when equal after normalising curly quotes to straight, en and em dashes to a hyphen and runs of whitespace to one space; case is kept.
{{q4.compute}}
- **Counts** are loops over the records in JavaScript; nothing is estimated and no model is called.

## How the app checks itself

Each check is one line: what was compared, the two values, and "pass" in green or "check failed" in red with a link to the rows concerned. A failed check never hides a result; it marks it.

- **Paragraph count.** Paragraphs found against `reference.paragraphs`.
- **Numbering.** The paragraph numbers are exactly 1 to n in order; gaps and duplicates are listed by number and page.
- **First words.** Each paragraph's first six words against `reference.first_words`; the count of mismatches, each listed as "para. n: found … / reference …", with the row flagged in the table.
{{q3.checks}}
{{q1.checks}}
- **Footnotes stay out of the paragraphs.** The first 40 characters of every line that opens a footnote, its number included ("15 Human Rights Committee, general comm…"; for a footnote whose number was displaced, its first line), are searched in the raw text of every paragraph, before footnote marks are touched (expected 0 hits; continuation lines are not searched, because a citation such as "United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change" also occurs in paragraph 6), and every paragraph over 300 words is listed (the longest real one has 254). A hit means a footnote block was read as body: the check fails, the paragraph is flagged in the table, and the "Paragraphs found" tile on tab 01 says "n contain footnotes" in red, even when the count is right.
- **Headers and footers.** Pages whose first line was the symbol (expected all); pages with a page number in the footer (expected all but the first); displaced footnote numbers, listed with their page.
- **Headings.** The number of labelled and unlabelled headings and the list of unlabelled ones, so a reader can spot a paragraph's last line mistaken for a heading.
- **Nothing lost.** Every non-empty line of every page is classified exactly once as cover, header, heading, paragraph, footnote or footer, and the counts per kind sum to the total non-empty lines in the file; any unclassified line is listed with its page and shown in red in the raw page viewer.

## Edge cases and risks

- A paragraph number on the same line as its text (2 of 90 here) and alone on its line (88) must both be accepted; handling one form only loses two paragraphs or finds none.
- "6 November 2025" on the cover starts with a number and a space; it is not a footnote because the counter is at 1 when it is met.
- The reference is a yardstick, not the truth: if the counts disagree, the app shows both and the difference, and never trims or pads its result to match.
- The first-words check sees six words; a paragraph can start correctly and be damaged later. The raw page viewer and the "Nothing lost" check cover the rest.
- If `reference` or one of its fields is missing, the tiles say "no reference in this file" and the checks that need it show "not run", never "pass".

## Design and accessibility

What this app adds to the studio look:

- **Red accent** on the active tab, the paragraph numbers in the first column, and the words "first words differ" and "check failed". "Pass" is dark green. Pass and fail are always words as well as colours.
- **Big serif numbers** only on the four tiles of tab 01, with paragraphs found beside the document's own count. Every table has a serif `<caption>` that states the message ("90 paragraphs found, 90 expected") and a monospace number (`TAB.01`).
- **Category colours** only in the raw page viewer: six pale tints (cover, header, heading, paragraph, footnote, footer), each doubled by a letter code in the margin and in the legend.
- Tables follow "Data visualisation: tables" (UK Government Analysis Function): `<th scope="col">`, numbers right-aligned, the source under the table, no footnotes inside data cells.
- The check panel follows "Quality assurance of code for analysis and research: Testing code" (Analysis Function): each check tells a story, given this data, having run this code, we expect this output; every repair has a named check.
- Explanations follow "GOV.UK content guidance: Clear language": short sentences; "footnote block", "footer" and "displaced number" explained the first time they appear.
- Citations follow the Dag Hammarskjöld Library's "How should I cite a UN document?": the symbol as the key, the paragraph as the pinpoint, the parts stored separately and formatted on copy.
- Keyboard: expandable rows and the repair log heading are buttons with `aria-expanded`; the tab panel of a hidden tab is not focusable.

## Out of scope

No model calls, no summaries, no OCR, no PDF rendering: the input is the converter's text. No lettered sub-paragraphs (none here), no editing in the browser, one document only.
